title: SpaceX Turns Carrier, and the Direct-to-Device Trade Pays the Price

html:
Market Overview

🌎 SpaceX Turns Carrier, and the Direct-to-Device Trade Pays the Price

Rising Treasury yields, which touched 5.35% on the 10-year midweek, their highest level since 2002, pressured growth and small-cap names across the sector on Wednesday and Thursday. The week's defining event, though, was sector-specific: SpaceX's agreement to acquire low-band wireless spectrum and build Starlink Mobile into a full U.S. carrier reshaped the competitive map for every direct-to-device satellite company in this basket, almost overnight.

That spectrum deal, and the uneven way it hit different stocks, is this week's Sentiment Signal below. Here is what moved the names with real, dated developments this week.

SpaceX (SPCX)

SpaceX's biggest news of the week had nothing to do with rockets. On Thursday, October 8, SpaceX agreed to acquire a nationwide portfolio of low-band 800 MHz spectrum, up to 14 MHz paired, from Grain Management, a deal aimed at turning Starlink Mobile into a full U.S. wireless carrier able to compete directly with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. Elon Musk called it a "very big deal," and all three incumbent carriers fell more than 6% in after-hours trading on the news, per CNBC and Benzinga. Reports on the deal's price conflicted: TradingKey put the value at roughly $8 billion in cash, while Benzinga described the price as undisclosed. We are flagging that discrepancy rather than reporting a single figure as confirmed. Wall Street kept raising its targets on SPCX even as the stock gave back ground. Morgan Stanley's Adam Jonas reiterated an Outperform rating and a $300 price target on Monday, October 5, calling the stock "cheap and getting cheaper." Goldman Sachs analyst Eric Sheridan raised his target from $220 to $230 on Tuesday, October 6, and Susquehanna lifted its target from $144 to $173 on Wednesday, October 7, while holding a Neutral rating. Cathie Wood's ARK Invest nonetheless trimmed its SPCX position twice during the week, selling 54,873 shares worth roughly $9.4 million on Tuesday and another 29,048 shares worth about $4.7 million on Thursday, per Benzinga. Separately, a Law360 roundup reported, without primary-source confirmation, that SpaceX is seeking financing for as much as $40 billion in Nvidia chip purchases to expand its AI compute footprint; we treat that figure as an unconfirmed rumor, not a company disclosure. On the hardware side, Starship stayed grounded for the week: Ship 42 had all six engines pulled for a third cryogenic proof test at Massey's, Ship 40 arrived at the Port of Brownsville on Wednesday, October 7, after a 75-day sea voyage, and the current FAA launch license still covers only Flight 14's planned ten-hour mission. SPCX shares eased from a Tuesday close of $171.92 to $162.57 by Friday, October 9, a decline of roughly 5.4% over those three sessions.

Rocket Lab (RKLB)

Rocket Lab drew a wave of conflicting analyst signals this week. Barclays initiated coverage with an Overweight rating and an $85 price target, dated to either Thursday, October 8 or Friday, October 9 depending on the tracker. A day or two later, MarketBeat and DefenseWorld both reported, citing Zacks, that Barclays had separately upgraded the stock to "Strong-Buy," a claim we treat with skepticism: "Strong-Buy" is Zacks' own quantitative ranking language, not standard Barclays terminology, and no primary Barclays note could be found reconciling an Overweight initiation with a Strong-Buy upgrade issued days later. TD Cowen's Gautam Khanna cut his price target to $90 from $120 on Friday, October 9, a move corroborated across two independent outlets. Shares fell alongside the broader sector on Tuesday, October 7, amid the rising-yield backdrop, though no RKLB-specific percentage for that day's move could be confirmed. Taken together, RKLB closed the week down roughly 6.6%, from $73.02 on Monday to $68.21 on Friday. The declines came despite a strong run of company news just before this window: a 20-launch Electron contract with Synspective announced September 30, Iridium shareholders' approval of Rocket Lab's roughly $8 billion acquisition of Iridium on September 24, and a fully funded $1.94 billion at-the-market equity raise completed September 15, none of which falls in this week but all of which remains the more important medium-term story for the stock.

AST SpaceMobile (ASTS)

AST SpaceMobile had the roughest week in the group, caught directly in SpaceX's spectrum crossfire. Shares fell as much as 15.4% intraday on Friday, October 9, closing down 10.48% at $50.97, near a 52-week low of $49.31, after SpaceX's Grain Management spectrum deal raised fears that Starlink Mobile could directly challenge AST's direct-to-device model, per two independent Benzinga reports. Earlier in the week shares had actually rallied: ASTS closed up 8% at $63.12 on Tuesday, October 6, which Benzinga attributed to investor focus on a potential $1 billion Japan opportunity tied to AST's joint venture with Rakuten, though we could not independently confirm that specific causal link. On Monday, October 5, AST and TELUS completed an initial integration test linking TELUS's terrestrial network to AST's satellites, a step toward direct-to-device service in Canada, confirmed by both Benzinga and Mobile World Live. Analyst sentiment stayed split: William Blair's Louie DiPalma reiterated a Hold on Monday, while Berenberg's Michael Filatov reiterated a Buy on Friday, per TipRanks, though neither note carried a stated price target this week. Over the full week, ASTS shares fell roughly 12.8%, from $58.44 on Monday to $50.97 on Friday.

Redwire (RDW)

Redwire landed a follow-on contract from Axiom Space on Monday, October 5, to supply two Roll-Out Solar Array wings for Axiom's second commercial space-station module, confirmed across four independent outlets including Business Wire and Seeking Alpha, though no dollar figure was disclosed. The stock fell 4.3% that same day regardless, then continued sliding through midweek amid the broader space-sector selloff on Wednesday, October 7, that also hit Rocket Lab and Intuitive Machines, per 24/7 Wall St. On Tuesday, October 6, CEO Peter Cannito told CNBC that the market is at "the start of massive growth in space," drawing a comparison to the historical rise of satellite television, though we could not independently verify his exact quoted language beyond the segment's headline. Redwire also filed a routine 8-K/A on Thursday, October 8, amending an earlier say-on-pay disclosure, a procedural filing with no new financial information. RDW shares fell from $10.43 on Monday to $9.58 by Friday, a weekly decline of roughly 8.1%.

Viasat (VSAT)

Viasat's week was dominated by routine insider paperwork rather than operating news. SEC filings show SVP Benjamin Palmer sold 2,000 shares worth $139,740 under a pre-existing trading plan, filed Monday, October 5, and officer Craig Miller filed notice to sell 11,893 shares worth roughly $851,629, filed Thursday, October 9. No company press release, 8-K, or analyst rating change was found dated within the week. Shares jumped 6.82% on Friday, October 9, to close at $72.01, though MarketBeat's own report on the move cited no specific catalyst, and we could not independently confirm that close against a second data source, so we flag it as single-sourced pending further verification. The stock had also fallen roughly 3.1% intraday on Monday, October 5, again without an identified cause.

MDA Space (MDA)

MDA Space CEO Mike Greenley appeared on CNBC on Thursday, October 8, arguing that Russian and Chinese hypersonic-missile development is fueling new demand for space-based missile defense, and separately that companies and nations are increasingly seeking alternatives to Starlink, a notable data point for the broader direct-to-device competitive story unfolding this week. No other dated company news, SEC or SEDAR filing, contract announcement, or analyst note was found within the window. MDA shares were volatile, falling from an opening C$42.54 on Monday to a low close of C$38.81 on Thursday, before rebounding 3.53% to close at C$40.18 on Friday, a net weekly decline of roughly 5.5% in Canadian dollars from Monday's open. No source identified a specific catalyst for either the Thursday low or the Friday rebound.

Planet Labs (PL)

Planet Labs had a volatile but ultimately directionless week. CNBC's Jim Cramer reportedly praised the company on Monday, October 5, saying he thought the stock was "done going down," which Benzinga credited, along with lingering momentum from an early-October satellite launch, for an intraday rally that pushed shares up as much as 5% on Tuesday, October 6, to a close of $18.57. That gain reversed by Thursday, October 8, when PL fell roughly 3.5% to 4% amid the broader risk-off move tied to the 10-year Treasury yield hitting 5.35% and an unconfirmed Financial Times report that SpaceX is seeking roughly $40 billion in new debt financing. PL shares closed the week at $17.18 on Friday, essentially flat from Monday's $17.36 close, a decline of about 1%. No SEC filing, analyst rating change, or new contract was confirmed within the window.

Firefly Aerospace (FLY)

Firefly Aerospace saw its board change hands this week: director Thomas Zurbuchen resigned effective September 30, and on Monday, October 5, the board appointed Rick Ambrose, former head of Lockheed Martin's space business, as his replacement, per an SEC 8-K filed Tuesday, October 6. Barclays initiated coverage on the stock with an Equal Weight rating and a $34 price target sometime between Thursday and Friday, October 8 or 9 (sources disagree on the exact day). Shares fell sharply over the week regardless, from an opening $23.26 on Monday to a close of $20.00 on Friday, a decline of roughly 14%, with no single news item identified as the cause; the stock fell on four of the week's five trading sessions. No Firefly Alpha launch, NASA contract, or litigation update was confirmed within the window.

BlackSky Technology (BKSY)

BlackSky announced a new six-figure Gen-3 On-Demand pilot contract with an unnamed international intelligence customer on Thursday, October 8, confirmed across three independent outlets tracing to the same underlying Business Wire release; no exact dollar figure or customer identity was disclosed. Shares dipped roughly 3.2% the day of the announcement and continued drifting lower through the week, closing at $20.92 on Friday, October 9 (MarketBeat separately reported $20.90, an immaterial two-cent discrepancy), down from a $21.80 open on Monday, a weekly decline of about 4%. No SEC filing, analyst rating change, or ARK Invest trading activity was found dated within the window.

Takeaway

This was a week where capital allocation, not launches, moved the sector. SpaceX's spectrum deal with Grain Management reframed the competitive map for direct-to-device satellite plays overnight, hitting AST SpaceMobile hardest while leaving Globalstar, already locked into its Amazon buyout, comparatively untouched. Rising Treasury yields added a macro headwind midweek that weighed on Planet Labs and other names without a clear company-specific driver of their own. Next week, watch for any primary-source confirmation of the Grain Management deal's price tag, resolution of Barclays' conflicting Rocket Lab rating actions, and whether AST SpaceMobile addresses the SpaceX spectrum threat directly on its next investor update.

Orbit Focus

🎯SPACEX'S SPECTRUM EARTHQUAKE: THE DIRECT-TO-DEVICE WAR JUST GOT REAL

For two years, the direct-to-device satellite story has been framed as a race between upstarts: AST SpaceMobile's standalone BlueBird constellation against SpaceX's Starlink Direct-to-Cell service, run as a feature bolted onto an existing broadband business, with Globalstar and smaller players filling in around the edges. This week, that framing broke. On Thursday, October 8, SpaceX said it had agreed to acquire a nationwide portfolio of low-band 800 MHz spectrum, up to 14 MHz paired, from spectrum investment firm Grain Management. The deal is not about adding a few more bars of signal to Starlink's existing phone service. It is about turning Starlink Mobile into a standalone U.S. wireless carrier that can sell service directly to consumers, competing head-on with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, not just supplementing them. The market's reaction over the following three trading days shows just how unevenly that shift lands across the space-equity sector, and offers a useful case study in how a single corporate action can simultaneously help one stock, crater another, and leave a third almost entirely untouched.

The deal itself. SpaceX's agreement with Grain Management covers a nationwide, low-band spectrum portfolio described by multiple outlets as up to 14 MHz of paired 800 MHz-band licenses, the kind of low-frequency spectrum prized for its ability to penetrate buildings and cover wide areas with fewer towers, exactly the profile a satellite-to-phone network needs to behave like a real carrier rather than a dead-zone patch. Elon Musk called it a "very big deal," and SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said the company intends to target existing wireless-carrier customers directly, according to Benzinga's reporting on the announcement. The reaction in traditional telecom was immediate: AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile shares each fell more than 6% in after-hours trading the same evening, per CNBC. What the deal actually cost SpaceX, however, is not settled. TradingKey reported a price of roughly $8 billion in cash; a separate Benzinga report on the same day described the price as undisclosed. Neither a company statement nor an SEC filing was located to resolve the conflict, so we are treating the $8 billion figure as unconfirmed rather than reporting it as fact. That a deal of this apparent magnitude could make it a full trading week later without a confirmed price tag is itself a reminder that SpaceX, still a young public company following its 2026 IPO, discloses on its own schedule, not a conventional one.

Who got hurt, and who got spared. The sharpest, cleanest reaction in the group belongs to AST SpaceMobile. ASTS fell as much as 15.4% intraday on Friday, October 9, closing down 10.48% at $50.97, within shouting distance of its 52-week low of $49.31, as investors concluded that a SpaceX armed with real carrier spectrum is a far more direct threat to AST's core business than a SpaceX merely bundling satellite texting into existing Starlink plans. Unlike SpaceX, or Viasat, or MDA Space, AST SpaceMobile has essentially one business: direct-to-device connectivity. It has no diversified enterprise satellite backlog, no government missile-defense contracts, no broadband subscriber base to fall back on if the carrier-style competition intensifies. That singular focus, which has been the bull case for AST SpaceMobile as the "pure play" on this theme, became the bear case in a single afternoon. Viasat, by contrast, actually rose 6.82% on the same Friday, closing at $72.01, with MarketBeat's own write-up on the move naming no specific catalyst. One read, impossible to confirm with the sourcing available this week but consistent with the pattern, is that investors differentiated between a diversified satellite operator with substantial government and enterprise revenue, Viasat, and a single-product direct-to-device pure play, AST SpaceMobile, even though both nominally compete in the same space. We flag that interpretation as analysis, not confirmed fact, since no outlet explicitly tied Viasat's move to the spectrum news.

One fund, two casualties, and a case study in correlation breaking down. A Benzinga report on AST SpaceMobile's Friday drop noted that the Procure Space ETF, ticker UFO, holds both SpaceX, at roughly 16.73% of the fund, and AST SpaceMobile, at roughly 4.86%, alongside Rocket Lab, EchoStar, and Viasat. That single data point captures the whole week in miniature: a thematic space-sector fund's two largest, most directly comparable satellite-communications holdings moved in opposite directions on the same piece of news, one because the news was good for it and one because the news was bad for it. Investors who bought UFO, or similar baskets, for diversified exposure to "satellite telecom" got a sharp lesson this week in how little diversification that theme actually provides once a single company's strategic move can simultaneously be a tailwind and a headwind for its own fund-mates.

Wall Street's split verdict, and a side note on timing. Even as ASTS absorbed the week's worst single-day drop in the group, sell-side analysts spent the same week raising targets on SpaceX itself: Morgan Stanley's Adam Jonas reiterated Outperform and a $300 target on Monday, calling SPCX "cheap and getting cheaper"; Goldman Sachs raised its target to $230 on Tuesday; Susquehanna raised its target to $173 on Wednesday, while keeping a Neutral rating. None of those three notes, based on the public reporting available, directly addressed the Grain Management deal, which had not yet been announced when the earliest of them was published. That sequencing matters: the spectrum deal landed in the middle of a week that was already bullish on SpaceX for unrelated reasons (described in SpaceX's Market Overview item above), which may have amplified the market's read of the deal as aggressive expansion from a position of strength, rather than a defensive move. Cathie Wood's ARK Invest, notably, trimmed its SpaceX position twice that same week, on Tuesday and again on Thursday, a reminder that even bullish long-term holders take profits into strength.

The Globalstar exception. If AST SpaceMobile is the week's clearest loser, Globalstar is the clearest non-participant. GSAT shares were essentially flat, closing at $83.82 on Friday, up a modest 0.72% on the day, with no identifiable reaction to the SpaceX news at all. The reason is structural rather than operational: Globalstar is not trading as an independent direct-to-device competitor anymore. It has been under a definitive acquisition agreement with Amazon since April 2026, with holders able to elect $90.00 per share in cash, capped at 40% of shares, or Amazon stock. A company already priced as a pending acquisition target, rather than as an ongoing competitive business, simply has less exposure to a rival's strategic news, good or bad. Globalstar's quiet week is not a sign that the SpaceX spectrum deal does not matter to the broader direct-to-device landscape; it is a sign that Globalstar has, in effect, already exited that landscape and is now trading on deal-completion risk and timeline instead.

Takeaway. The SpaceX-Grain Management spectrum deal is a reminder that in this sector, the biggest risk to a direct-to-device pure play is not a technical failure or a missed launch window, it is a much larger, better-capitalized competitor deciding to build the exact same thing with more resources. AST SpaceMobile's 12.8% weekly decline and Viasat's same-week rally show that the market is already differentiating between diversified satellite operators and single-product bets on this theme, even within the same thematic ETFs. Watch for three things next week: whether SpaceX or Grain Management discloses an actual deal price, whether AST SpaceMobile's management responds publicly to the competitive read, and whether other direct-to-device or satellite-telecom names see analyst notes specifically addressing their exposure to a SpaceX that is no longer just a rocket company, but now a prospective nationwide wireless carrier as well.
